disagreements.about: whether a stressed syllable on a swung offbeat is a problem
disagreements.position: the words come first; a stress against the beat is a flag
disagreements.settledBy: the weak-beat stress rate over the line, against the swing figure
disagreements.theirs: the swing puts the offbeat where it belongs; the words fit the beat

disagreements.about: whether a vocal sample counts as a lyric
disagreements.position: if the words are heard they are lyrics and they are read
disagreements.settledBy: intelligibility: a chop with a whole phrase is the Lyricist's too
disagreements.theirs: a chopped voice is a sound; its words are texture

disagreements.about: whether the bass should leave room under the vocal
disagreements.position: a busy line under a dense verse fights the words
disagreements.settledBy: attacks per bar under a sung line: six, the verse budget, and rest on the stressed syllables
disagreements.theirs: the line sits behind the kick and under the voice by register, not by resting

disagreements.about: whether the words serve the brief or the brief serves the words
disagreements.position: the song is about what the words say it is about, once they are sung
disagreements.settledBy: the title: if the hook line and the brief disagree, the brief is rewritten, once
disagreements.theirs: the brief is one sentence and the words are measured against it

disagreements.about: whether the vocal should be loud enough to read
disagreements.position: every word is heard, or it was not worth writing
disagreements.settledBy: intelligibility as the Lyricist reads it back from the bounce: the stressed syllables audible
disagreements.theirs: the vocal sits in the mix where the record's idiom puts it, and lo-fi buries it a little

disagreements.about: whether the hook is the words or the section
disagreements.position: the hook is the line the listener sings back, and the section is named for it
disagreements.settledBy: the title line: if it lands in the section the Peer names, both are right
disagreements.theirs: the hook is when the song arrives, wherever the title falls

disagreements.about: whether the words or the chords decide where a phrase ends
disagreements.position: the line ends where the breath does, and the chords can wait a bar for it
disagreements.settledBy: the section's last bar: both end there, and inside it the line may cross a change
disagreements.theirs: the cadence is where the phrase ends, and a line that runs past it is running past the harmony

lineages.instrument: the stress mark and the rhyme table
lineages.name: Pat Pattison
lineages.why: The craft is codified: Writing Better Lyrics and the Berklee prosody courses state rhyme types — perfect, family, additive, subtractive, assonance, consonance — stress against the beat, and line-to-line matching as rules a reader can apply to any lyric, which is exactly what a persona needs.

lineages.name: Jimmy Webb
lineages.why: Tunesmith is a working songwriter's account of the same craft from the inside — the syllable count of a sung line, the title as the hook's line, the internal rhyme that carries a verse — with Wichita Lineman and MacArthur Park to check every claim against by ear.

lineages.name: Sheila Davis
lineages.why: The Craft of Lyric Writing is the earlier codification the other two build on: it states the forms (AABA, verse-chorus) and the rhyme-scheme conventions as conventions, with the scheme letters a reader writes in the margin, which is what a scheme reader implements.

openQuestions.alternative: The floor should be per stanza type — a verse needs eight tenths, a bridge is allowed to break the shape on purpose — and the reading should say which it is in.
openQuestions.encoded: Six tenths: below it a listener hears a different line, above it the same tune fits.
openQuestions.question: Is six tenths the right floor for two lines to share a shape?

openQuestions.alternative: Assume the meter — a stressed syllable every other beat — and read against that, marked as a guess, so the writer hears the flag before the tune exists.
openQuestions.encoded: No: without a melody the reading is line against line, and the beat rule waits for alignment.
openQuestions.question: Can stress be read against the beat before the lyric is aligned to a melody?

openQuestions.alternative: A voice is exactly the images a writer returns to, and the rule should read the ratio of returning images rather than count any one — a house with no repeated image has no voice.
openQuestions.encoded: Three: twice is a motif, three times the writer cannot see it.

openQuestions.question: Is an image in three songs a tic, or a voice?

openQuestions.alternative: Sung stress follows the melody, not the dictionary, and a word's stress should be read from the note it lands on when the lyric is aligned — the dictionary only when it is not.
openQuestions.encoded: Yes, as the default: CMUdict's primary stress is the spoken stress, and a singer starts there.
